extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties to PTAB inter partes review proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, and their counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for (1) instituting an inter partes review under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) and (2) joining a petitioner to an instituted IPR under 35 U.S.C. § 315(c), including discretionary factors (General Plastic), timing limits, and related-practice considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inter partes review may not be instituted "unless . . . there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory threshold the Board uses to decide whether to institute review; even if the merits suggest unpatentability, the Board may exercise its discretion under § 314(a) to deny institution (see General Plastic discretionary analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time bar under 35 U.S.C. § 315(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inter partes review may not be instituted if the petition requesting the proceeding is filed more than 1 year after the date on which the petitioner, real party in interest, or privy of the petitioner is served with a complaint alleging infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The § 315(b) time limitation prevents late petitions; however, the statute provides that this time limitation "shall not apply to a request for joinder under subsection (c)." Parties must assess whether a petition is time-barred unless joinder exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder statutory standard under 35 U.S.C. § 315(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director, in his or her discretion, may join as a party to that inter partes review any person who properly files a petition under section 311 that the Director . . . determines warrants the institution of an inter partes review under section 314.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joinder requires two determinations (per Facebook v. Windy City): (1) whether the joinder applicant’s petition 'warrants' institution under § 314, and (2) if it does, whether to join the applicant as a party. A petition that does not warrant institution cannot be the basis for joinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic Factor 1: prior petition by same petitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the same petitioner previously filed a petition directed to the same claims of the same patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the petitioner has previously filed an earlier petition challenging the same claims, this factor weighs in favor of denying institution under the Board's discretionary authority. Prior denials (even discretionary) and repeated filings are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic Factor 2: petitioner knowledge of prior art at time of first petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether at the time of filing of the first petition the petitioner knew of the prior art asserted in the second petition or should have known of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor assesses whether the petitioner could or should have raised the challenges earlier; if petitioner knew (or should have known) of the asserted art earlier, that may weigh toward denying a later petition unless justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic Factor 3: petitioner’s access to prior responses/decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether at the time of filing of the second petition the petitioner already received the patent owner’s preliminary response to the first petition or received the Board’s decision on whether to institute review in the first petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor guards against 'road mapping'—taking advantage of an opponent’s filings or Board decisions to improve a later petition. Evidence that a later petition was modified based on earlier responses/decisions weighs against institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic Factor 4: time between learning of prior art and filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of time that elapsed between the time the petitioner learned of the prior art asserted in the second petition and the filing of the second petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long delays without adequate explanation suggest the petitioner should have raised the challenge earlier and weigh in favor of discretionary denial; shorter, reasonably diligent timing may weigh against denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic Factor 5: petitioner’s explanation for delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the petitioner provides adequate explanation for the time elapsed between the filings of multiple petitions directed to the same claims of the same patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A persuasive, adequate explanation for delay (e.g., newly discovered art, reliance on pending institution decisions) can mitigate concerns and weigh against discretionary denial. Lack of explanation supports denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic Factor 6: finite resources of the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: The finite resources of the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board considers its limited resources when deciding whether to institute multiple proceedings on the same patent; absent a petitioner-provided ranking or rationale for multiple petitions (as urged by the Trial Practice Guide), expenditure of resources on repeated or duplicative petitions weighs against institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic Factor 7: one-year final determination requirement (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(11))
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(11) to issue a final determination not later than 1 year after the date on which the Director notices institution of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution and joinder that would likely disrupt schedules or make it difficult to meet the one-year statutory target (or otherwise create significant scheduling complexity) weighs in favor of discretionary denial; joining late or adding parties can adversely affect timely resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Practice Guide guidance on multiple petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board’s Consolidated Trial Practice Guide provides guidance on multiple petitions, instructing petitioners to provide a ranking between petitions and information why additional petitions should be instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple petitions challenge the same patent, petitioners should explain the need and rank petitions to help the Board allocate resources; failure to provide such ranking or rationale may weigh against institution or joinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of related district-court litigation (Fintiv-related concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may consider related district-court litigation and whether institution/joinder would duplicate or redo work done in that litigation or otherwise affect judicial economy and schedule (as under Fintiv precedent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include existence of a stay, prior jury verdicts on same prior art, overlapping issues, potential to redo district-court work, and the effect on Board scheduling; significant overlap with district-court proceedings can favor denial of institution or joinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (or absence) of stipulations re: not raising IPR grounds at trial (Sand Revolution II guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Board guidance (e.g., Sand Revolution II) approves use of stipulations by parties agreeing not to raise IPR grounds at district-court trial; failure to proffer such a stipulation where appropriate can weigh strongly against institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If petitioner had the opportunity to offer a stipulation (agreeing not to assert at trial the same grounds) but did not, that omission can be a strong reason to exercise discretion to deny institute/joinder, especially when earlier guidance on such stipulations was available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on continuing a proceeding that would otherwise be terminated (Uniloc concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may deny joinder where granting joinder would permit a petitioner to 'stand in' to continue a proceeding that would otherwise be terminated (e.g., due to settlement of the original petitioner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If joinder would effectively continue an instituted proceeding that the original petitioner has terminated by settlement, the Board may view that as an inappropriate use of joinder and deny the motion (see Uniloc precedent).
